docs.title: PN51 Homelab
docs.text:
Terraform creates four Ubuntu 26.04 LTS guests on Proxmox. Ansible installs Ubuntu Desktop, configures a one-server/three-worker K3s cluster, and deploys Prometheus and Grafana through the pinned kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart.

Start with provisioning. For an existing installation, use operations or monitoring.

Need Guide Build the lab from a prepared host Provisioning tutorial Understand ownership and failure modes Architecture Look up inputs, versions, and commands Reference Replace a worker or restore state Operations Keep a public repository safe Security Check correctness and convergence Testing

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
The PN51 has 32 GiB RAM and a 1 TB NVMe disk. Four 6 GiB desktop VMs leave 8 GiB for Proxmox. Each VM has two vCPUs and an 80 GiB root disk.

This is one physical failure domain. The control plane uses a single-member embedded etcd datastore for snapshots, not for high availability. Monitoring uses node-local persistent volumes by default. Back up both cluster state and application data outside this machine.

docs.title: Optional Application GitOps
docs.text:
The infrastructure bootstrap does not install Argo CD or deploy the existing fitness-tracker example. Ansible owns the monitoring Helm release so that its CRDs, secret boundary, and recovery path remain available without an application GitOps controller.

If you later add Argo CD, keep its ownership separate from Terraform and the Ansible-managed monitoring release. Do not let two reconcilers manage the same objects. Review the example Application's automated sync/prune behavior, image versions, namespace, service exposure, and application credentials before applying it.

The existing application's Secret has empty values and is not a production secret source. Use a dedicated encrypted-secret or external-secret workflow for real applications; public Git must not contain populated plaintext Secret data. Base64-encoding a Kubernetes Secret is not protection.

Public ingress, TLS, authentication, external DNS, application database backups, and network policies are separate explicit additions. The base cluster disables the default K3s ingress and service-load-balancer controllers and opens no NodePort range.

See security, architecture, and operations.

docs.title: How to Use Monitoring
docs.text: The Ansible monitoring role installs a SHA-256-pinned kube-prometheus-stack archive. It includes Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, kube-state-metrics, node-exporter, dashboards, rules, and Prometheus Operator CRDs.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Complete provisioning. Use the private administrator kubeconfig on a trusted controller. This is not a public dashboard installation.

docs.title: How to Open Grafana
docs.text:
In a dedicated terminal:

kubectl --kubeconfig .local/kubeconfig -n monitoring port-forward \
    --address 127.0.0.1 service/monitoring-grafana 3000:80

Open http://127.0.0.1:3000. The default username is admin; the generated password is in the encrypted vault. Retrieve it through your trusted local vault workflow, not a public terminal transcript or chat. Do not bind forwarding to 0.0.0.0.

Dashboards supplied by the chart are available immediately. Grafana's data and customizations persist on its 2 GiB PVC. Its admin password is initialized in the database; changing only the bootstrap Secret does not rotate an existing account.

docs.title: How to Open Prometheus or Alertmanager
docs.text:
Use separate terminals as needed:

kubectl --kubeconfig .local/kubeconfig -n monitoring port-forward \
    --address 127.0.0.1 service/monitoring-prometheus 9090:9090

kubectl --kubeconfig .local/kubeconfig -n monitoring port-forward \
    --address 127.0.0.1 service/monitoring-alertmanager 9093:9093

Open http://127.0.0.1:9090 or http://127.0.0.1:9093. These services have no independent public authentication boundary and must stay private. Stop each forward with Ctrl-C when finished.

Prometheus retains up to three days or about 8 GB in a 12 GiB PVC. Its WAL and compaction need space beyond the retention-size setting. Alertmanager uses 1 GiB for silences and notification state. No alert email/webhook destination is invented; configure a receiver and its credentials deliberately when required.

docs.title: How to Check Health
docs.text:
make verify
kubectl --kubeconfig .local/kubeconfig -n monitoring get pods,pvc,services
kubectl --kubeconfig .local/kubeconfig -n monitoring get prometheus,alertmanager

Expect private ClusterIP services, three Bound persistent claims, ready operator and exporters, and ready Prometheus/Alertmanager instances. Inspect Prometheus Status > Targets when a scrape fails. The workflow disables etcd, controller-manager, scheduler, and kube-proxy monitors/rules that do not map to this default K3s installation; it does not open their bind addresses just to make dashboards green.

Node-exporter inspects the host but uses pod networking rather than a host metrics listener. The monitoring namespace explicitly permits privileged pod security for host inspection; do not admit unrelated or untrusted workloads.

docs.title: How to Change Retention or Storage
docs.text:
Edit the non-secret monitoring values and run make chart-check, then make configure and make verify. Review the resource reference before increasing requests or retention on this 32 GiB host.

To use external storage, install and validate that storage class separately and set the Ansible variable monitoring_storage_class. Changing the variable does not migrate an existing PVC. Back up and restore data through a planned storage migration; PVC storage class and many volume fields are immutable.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Check Prometheus/Alertmanager Pending PVC binding, worker scheduling, local-path helper pod events, memory and disk Grafana unavailable after restart Its Deployment, bound PVC, node affinity, database health, and permissions Targets down Endpoint discovery, kubelet TLS/authentication, CNI traffic, and VM firewall state Chart checksum mismatch Stop; verify the reviewed version/hash pair and inspect the cached archive CRD conflict on upgrade Review upstream migrations and current field ownership; do not force conflicts blindly Data disappeared after VM replacement Local-path data is on the old VM disk; restore from off-host backup Old Grafana password still works Existing database password is separate from the bootstrap Secret

See backup and recovery, security, and live acceptance.

docs.title: How to Operate and Rebuild the Lab
docs.text: These procedures assume the provisioning tutorial has completed and the live acceptance checks pass. Keep an independent controller and off-host backups; the PN51 must not be its own only recovery environment.

docs.title: How to Reconcile Desired State
docs.text:
make plan
make configure
make verify

Apply Terraform only when the reviewed plan contains intended VM changes. A normal Ansible run repairs declared package/file/service state without rebooting or unconditionally upgrading everything. If you changed Terraform networking, regenerate inventory and inspect connectivity before configuring guests.

Do not change node names, pod/service CIDRs, or the server token in a running cluster as routine configuration. These values are cluster identity, not casual tuning knobs.

docs.title: How to Replace a Worker
docs.text:
1. Check backups and identify the generated worker name with kubectl --kubeconfig .local/kubeconfig get nodes -o wide.
  2. Run make replace-worker NODE=pn51-worker-2.
  3. Inspect the saved Terraform plan. The helper rejects changes outside that worker and its firewall resources. Type the exact confirmation only when destroying its root disk is intended.
  4. After replacement, open the new VM's Proxmox console and verify its SSH host fingerprint. Remove only the old address's known_hosts entry after confirming this was an expected rebuild, then accept the new verified key.
  5. Run make configure, make verify, and make idempotence.

The helper requires the server and remaining workers to be Ready. It refuses node-affined or uncertain local persistent volumes before draining. A released or retained PV can still hold data and can still block replacement. It respects pod disruption budgets and does not use forced eviction. EmptyDir data is explicitly disposable and is deleted by drain.

After a successful Terraform replacement, it deletes the old Kubernetes Node and waits for K3s to remove the corresponding node-password Secret. The new guest can then rejoin with the same stable node name. Never manually erase an active worker's identity just to make a join succeed.

docs.title: Data-Bearing Workers
docs.text:
The default local-path provisioner stores data under /var/lib/rancher/k3s/storage on one VM. A persistent volume's node affinity prevents it from following a pod to a different worker. Kubernetes rescheduling is not a storage migration.

For data-bearing workers, first use a workload-specific backup/restore or migrate to an existing off-host storage class. Verify restored data, remove obsolete claims/PVs only when their contents are no longer needed, and rerun the guarded procedure. Do not remove affinity or delete PVs merely to bypass its warning.

docs.title: How to Update Software
docs.text:
Take and verify backups first. Update one ownership layer at a time:

Layer Procedure Controller dependencies Review project changes, run uv lock, commit lockfile, run make setup check Provider Review release notes and planned replacements; update provider pin and lockfile; run mock tests Ubuntu base image Choose a dated official image, verify signed checksums, update URL/hash, review replacement plan Ubuntu guest packages Use a drained, one-at-a-time maintenance window for upgrades and required reboots K3s Review supported upgrade path and release checksum, change version/hash together, run offline and live tests Monitoring Review chart/Grafana/operator upgrade notes, update version/hash together, render/check CRD changes

K3s server changes happen before workers. The single API server can be unavailable during restart; workers are processed one at a time and drained only when their K3s binary/config/unit changes. Existing disruption budgets can legitimately stop an upgrade. Never bypass them without understanding the affected workload.

Guest security updates run unattended, but automatic reboots are disabled. During maintenance, drain the selected worker, upgrade packages, reboot if required, wait for Ready, uncordon, and verify workloads before moving to the next. A server reboot is a planned API outage. Desktop packages are not frozen by the cloud-image pin; current security packages come from Ubuntu's repositories.

The role reconciles chart CRDs separately with server-side apply. Conflicts are not force-overwritten. Helm's atomic rollback does not roll back CRDs, databases, or PVC data; follow upstream migration requirements and keep backups.

docs.title: How to Back Up
docs.text:
Back up these independent layers:

Layer Required off-host material Terraform State and backup, private tfvars/backend configuration, provider lockfile Controller Encrypted vault, separate vault password, SSH key recovery, trusted CA details K3s etcd snapshot plus the original server token and configuration Applications Database-native backups and persistent volume contents Hypervisor Proxmox configuration and tested VM backups to independent storage

K3s takes a local embedded-etcd snapshot every six hours and retains 14. Those snapshots are lost with the server disk unless exported. Create a manual snapshot through the verified server SSH connection before a change:

sudo /usr/local/bin/k3s etcd-snapshot save --name before-maintenance
sudo /usr/local/bin/k3s etcd-snapshot ls

These are guest commands, not controller commands. Export snapshots from /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/db/snapshots to encrypted storage on another machine. Protect the original token with them; losing it can make a snapshot unusable. Configure K3s S3 snapshot support separately if you want automatic off-host exports. This repository does not invent an S3 endpoint or silently claim off-host backup automation.

An etcd snapshot contains Kubernetes objects, not Grafana's SQLite database, Prometheus's TSDB, or arbitrary PV files. Quiesce or use each application's documented backup mechanism. Use Proxmox Backup Server on independent storage for VM-level protection where available, and test restoration into isolated VM IDs and a non-conflicting network.

docs.title: How to Recover the Control Plane
docs.text:
The automated worker helper refuses the server. Server replacement needs the original vault/token, the relevant etcd snapshot, preserved addressing, and a separate restore window.

  1. Stop the old server permanently and prevent it from coming back with the same address. Preserve its disk for investigation if possible.
  2. Restore a tested Proxmox backup, or provision a fresh Ubuntu 26.04 guest at the declared identity. Verify its SSH fingerprint. Do not blindly run normal configuration against an empty datastore: that would create a new cluster.
  3. Install the same pinned K3s version and baseline. Securely restore the original root token/config files and place the snapshot on the guest.
  4. Follow the upstream single-server snapshot restore procedure. With K3s stopped, use its explicit server --cluster-reset --cluster-reset-restore-path=/absolute/snapshot/path operation, the original token, and the original configuration. This is a manual recovery action, not a normal service flag; do not leave cluster-reset in the systemd unit.
  5. Start K3s normally. Verify restored node identities and resources before reconciling anything. Existing workers should connect to the restored API; investigate identities rather than deleting them blindly.
  6. Export a fresh administrator kubeconfig, reconcile desired state, restore PV data as needed, then run make verify and make idempotence.

Keep recovery instructions matched to the pinned release and test them in an isolated lab. A full restore has not been proven merely because an offline unit test passes.

docs.title: How to Rebuild Everything
docs.text:
Take off-host backups and verify recoverability. make destroy requires normal Terraform confirmation and deletes the managed VMs, their disks, and the managed base image. Local ignored files are not automatically erased. Review the full destroy plan before confirming.

For an intentionally empty new cluster, apply again, verify new SSH fingerprints, and configure from the preserved private inputs. For recovery, restore etcd and application data instead of allowing a fresh cluster to replace the old one. Never discard Terraform state while the corresponding resources still exist: restore the state or import the exact existing resources first.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Failure Safe response Drain blocked Inspect disruption budgets and replica health; do not force eviction by default Replacement stops after VM apply Inspect saved plan/state and new VM; finish verified identity cleanup and provisioning Replacement blocked by PV Migrate or restore its data before deleting its VM Node remains cordoned after interruption Confirm node health, then explicitly uncordon it API lost after server rebuild Restore the original datastore/token; do not join workers to an unintended new cluster Helm upgrade rollback fails Inspect CRD and data migrations separately from release rollback

See security, reference, and live acceptance.

docs.title: Build the Four-VM Lab
docs.text: This tutorial starts with a prepared Proxmox host and ends with four Ubuntu Desktop VMs, K3s, and private Prometheus/Grafana services. No step below is run automatically by CI. Commands are run on your trusted administrator workstation.

docs.title: What You Need
docs.text:
• PN51 with 32 GiB RAM, sufficient free NVMe capacity, AMD virtualization enabled, and reliable wired networking.
  • Proxmox VE 9 installed and patched, with a working private bridge. Back up the current PN51 before installing it: installation can erase existing disks.
  • Four unused VM IDs and four reserved IPv4 addresses outside the DHCP pool.
  • A trusted Proxmox HTTPS certificate or its CA installed on the controller.
  • Terraform 1.10+, uv, Helm 3, kubectl compatible with the pinned Kubernetes minor, OpenSSH, Git, and Make. Gitleaks and actionlint are useful for CI checks.
  • An existing SSH key loaded into ssh-agent. Keep its private half outside this repository.

The sibling dotfiles project is the source of truth for your workstation and guest user environment. Its macOS workstation setup includes Terraform, uv, Ansible, Helm 3, kubectl, Gitleaks, and actionlint. From the homelab checkout:

cd ../dotfiles
./bootstrap.sh --platform macos --profile personal --dry-run
./bootstrap.sh --platform macos --profile personal
cd ../homelab

Review and confirm its plan; this is your normal full MacBook setup, not a reduced VM package installation. Use the work profile when appropriate. If you already manage the controller with dotfiles, do not reinstall it just to run homelab: check the required executable versions and run make setup here.

If an old Helm 4 binary shadows Helm 3, fix PATH before continuing. Check helm version --short and kubectl version --client against the version reference.

docs.title: Step 1: Validate the Controller
docs.text:
make setup
make check

These commands do not need a vault, Proxmox token, or reachable VMs. You should see nine passing Terraform mock tests, Python regressions, four local template checks, a real Helm render, and a strict documentation build.

If collection installation reports CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED, use a verified host CA bundle, for example on macOS:

SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/cert.pem UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=true make setup

Do not bypass certificate verification. If your organization's CA is absent, install it through the operating system's trust workflow first.

docs.title: Step 2: Prepare Proxmox
docs.text:
In the Proxmox UI, confirm the node name, bridge, and storage identifiers. The disk datastore must support VM disks. Enable Import content on the file-backed image datastore; the Terraform image uses a .qcow2 filename.

Enable the datacenter firewall and verify that it is active. Preserve a working Proxmox console and management rule before changing host-level firewall policy. Terraform only manages the four new VM firewalls, never datacenter or host firewall rules. A VM firewall flag alone is not sufficient when the datacenter firewall is disabled.

Create a dedicated, privilege-separated API token for Terraform. Grant VM allocation, audit, power, console, and configuration permissions for the reserved VM IDs, and allocation/audit permissions on the chosen datastores and bridge. The provider's download-url endpoint also needs Sys.Audit, Sys.Modify, and Datastore.AllocateTemplate; review those host-level privileges explicitly. Do not use the root password or a permanent unrestricted Administrator token. Remove bootstrap-only image-download privileges after initial provisioning if your operational policy requires it; re-grant or import the existing image when rebuilding from empty state.

The token owner and privilege-separated token both need the applicable ACLs. A 403 is a permissions problem, not a reason to disable TLS. See the provider's authentication documentation and Proxmox's permission model. Exact ACLs must be validated on your host; offline tests cannot prove them.

docs.title: Step 3: Set Private Inputs and Preview
docs.text:
cp pn51/terraform/terraform.tfvars.example pn51/terraform/terraform.tfvars
chmod 600 pn51/terraform/terraform.tfvars

Edit the private copy. Set your real LAN, gateway, trusted administrator /32 or subnet, Proxmox node, datastores, and SSH public key. Example addresses are not network discovery. The default pod/service networks must also be distinct from your VPN and other routed networks.

Load the endpoint and token into your current controller session. The following prompts for the credential without storing it in shell history; do not run it with shell tracing enabled:

export PROXMOX_VE_ENDPOINT='https://YOUR-VERIFIED-PROXMOX-HOST:8006/'
export PROXMOX_VE_API_TOKEN="$(uv run --frozen python -c 'import getpass; print(getpass.getpass("Proxmox API token: ")))"
make plan

The token format is user@realm!token-id=secret. A password manager can populate the same environment variable instead. Do not put this token in tfvars, a committed .env, a screenshot, a support transcript, or GitHub Actions secrets.

Inspect the plan: it should create four VMs, the base-image import, and their VM firewall resources. It must not modify the existing host or unrelated VMs.

docs.title: Step 4: Create VMs and Verify SSH Identity
docs.text:
make apply
make inventory

Confirm Terraform's plan interactively. It downloads the fixed Ubuntu image, checks its SHA-256, and creates each guest with static networking and your public key. Terraform does not wait for guest-agent installation: the first Ansible run installs and starts it after SSH becomes available.

For each VM, use the Proxmox console to read its SSH host fingerprint:

ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub

From your controller, connect as ubuntu and compare that fingerprint before accepting it into known_hosts. Do not use StrictHostKeyChecking=no, and do not trust an unauthenticated ssh-keyscan by itself. Cloud-init supplies passwordless sudo for this automation account; protect the corresponding key.

Check trusted connectivity after accepting all four identities:

uv run --frozen ansible k3s_cluster -m ansible.builtin.ping

docs.title: Step 5: Create and Back Up the Vault
docs.text:
make vault

Type the vault password directly into the terminal. The helper creates a random K3s server token and Grafana password, passes them to ansible-vault through stdin, and writes only encrypted output to .local/vault.yml with mode 0600. It refuses to overwrite an existing vault. Store the password separately in a password manager and back up the encrypted file off-host before configuring K3s.

For desktop console login, edit the vault and add desktop_password_hash as a quoted SHA-512-crypt or yescrypt hash:

uv run --frozen ansible-vault edit .local/vault.yml

Generate the hash with a trusted local password tool such as mkpasswd and enter the password interactively. Never use a plaintext password or Terraform password input. Use the vault editor on a trusted workstation; editor swap and recovery files can contain decrypted data. Omit the field to keep console login locked.

docs.title: Step 6: Configure Desktop, Kubernetes, and Monitoring
Optional Guest Dotfiles
docs.text:
Dotfiles deployment is disabled by default. The example pins the published dotfiles commit b703d09fe26c5bd7e9daac92450f3c313a4c7c6a, which includes the homelab package set, configuration checks, and official kubectl assets. Its published CI run passed. Keep a reviewed full commit SHA, never main or HEAD. Uncommitted sibling changes are deliberately not copied onto guests.

cp pn51/ansible/config.example.yml .local/config.yml
chmod 600 .local/config.yml

Review the private copy and its personal/work profile selection. The pinned commit is ready to use. The role uses the public dotfiles Git URL, deploys as ubuntu, and reads its lightweight package list and checksum-pinned kubectl from that revision. System hardening, Desktop installation, K3s, and monitoring remain homelab-owned. Your controller's private environment, SSH keys, and administrator kubeconfig are never copied to the guests. GNOME shortcuts remain a separate interactive choice.

Enable the integration with:

make configure CONFIG_FILE=.local/config.yml

Use the same CONFIG_FILE for later configuration and idempotence checks. To keep the original cluster-only setup, omit it:

make configure

The playbook validates that all targets are Ubuntu 26.04 x86-64 VMs. It waits for cloud-init before apt, installs full Desktop, disables sleep and swap, configures SSH and kernel settings, then starts K3s on the server and joins workers serially. The first Desktop installation can take several minutes per guest.

The server's administrator kubeconfig is copied to .local/kubeconfig with mode 0600 and a TLS-verified external endpoint. The controller then reconciles the chart's CRDs and Grafana Secret and installs the monitoring chart atomically. The token never enters a service command line or Terraform state.

docs.title: Step 7: Accept the Installation
docs.text:
make verify
make idempotence

With guest dotfiles enabled, use make idempotence CONFIG_FILE=.local/config.yml so both runs cover that role. make kube-shell opens an interactive controller shell with only this lab's private kubeconfig selected. Leaving that shell restores your original context; it does not change your global shell files or copy credentials to a VM.

verify checks the exact four node identities and K3s versions, Ready status, monitoring workloads, Bound persistent volumes, Grafana database health, Prometheus scrape targets, and the chart's Helm test. idempotence performs a normal run followed by a full second run that must report zero changes and no hidden failures on all four hosts. It can prompt for the vault password twice.

Use monitoring access for loopback-only port forwarding. Before using real workloads, configure and test off-host backups.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Action Proxmox returns 403 Inspect token-owner and token ACLs, storage permissions, and download privileges Import fails Enable Import content and check free space, filename, checksum, and Proxmox version SSH host key is unknown Compare through the Proxmox console; accept only the verified fingerprint Cloud-init fails or apt is locked Inspect cloud-init status --long and its logs; do not delete apt lockfiles A target is not Ubuntu 26.04 Stop and correct the image/inventory; do not weaken the assertion Worker name already exists Use the guarded replacement procedure, not forced node-password deletion Token mismatch Restore the original vault; do not invent a new token for the old datastore Monitoring stays Pending Check PVC binding, worker RAM/disk, local-path provisioner, and pod events

docs.title: What You Built
docs.text: You have four declaratively managed Desktop VMs, a private K3s cluster, and persistent monitoring. Continue with operations, security, and the reference. The live gates are what establish that this works on your actual PN51; offline CI alone does not.

docs.title: Configuration and Command Reference
docs.text: Run commands from the repository root. Relative inventory, role, collection, and local-artifact paths depend on that working directory.

docs.title: Versions and Artifacts
docs.text:
Component Pin or supported range Location Proxmox VE 9.x prerequisite Existing hypervisor; not installed by automation Terraform >= 1.10, < 2; CI uses 1.16.6 Terraform required-version constraint Proxmox provider bpg/proxmox 0.116.1 Terraform versions and provider lockfile Ubuntu base 26.04 amd64, build 20260927 Terraform image URL and SHA-256 Desktop Full ubuntu-desktop metapackage Baseline role; current packages from Ubuntu repositories K3s v1.37.1+k3s1 Ansible group variables; binary SHA-256 Helm 3.x; CI uses 3.22.1 Local CLI and CI setup Monitoring chart 92.9.0 Ansible group variables; archive SHA-256 Python 3.13 or 3.14; CI uses 3.13 Project constraint and uv.lock Ansible Core 2.20.6 Project dependencies and uv.lock Collections ansible.posix 2.1.0, kubernetes.core 6.1.0 Ansible requirements

Image and binary pins are immutable inputs, not permission to ignore security updates. Ubuntu's package repositories evolve; package installation is convergent, not a bit-for-bit image build. Review and update version/checksum pairs together, commit lockfiles, then run all tests and the live gates.

docs.title: Terraform Inputs
docs.text:
Copy the example into ignored pn51/terraform/terraform.tfvars and replace its public-key placeholder. It is deliberately invalid until a real public key is provided.

Input Type Default Constraint or behavior proxmox_node string required Existing Proxmox node name network_cidr string required Canonical IPv4 LAN/VLAN subnet gateway string required Usable address inside the node subnet admin_cidrs set(string) required Trusted IPv4 networks; no /0 ssh_public_keys list(string) required OpenSSH public keys, not paths or private keys vm_datastore string local-lvm Supports VM and cloud-init disks image_datastore string local File-backed; enable Import content bridge string vmbr0 Pre-existing private bridge cluster_name string pn51 2-32 lowercase DNS-safe characters vm_id_start number 5100 Integer 100-999999996; reserves four consecutive IDs node_ip_offset number 40 Four usable consecutive addresses, excluding gateway dns_servers list(string) 1.1.1.1, 9.9.9.9 At least one reachable IPv4 resolver vm_memory_mb number 6144 Integer, at least 6144; multiplied by four vm_disk_gb number 80 Integer, at least 48; disks cannot be shrunk safely pod_cidr string 10.42.0.0/16 IPv4 prefix at most /22; immutable on a running cluster service_cidr string 10.43.0.0/16 IPv4 prefix at most /24; immutable on a running cluster

The node, pod, and service networks must not overlap. Check router, VPN, and remote-site networks too: Terraform cannot discover your external routing table. Keep guest addresses outside DHCP and reserve IDs before the first apply.

Changing the cluster name, network identity, imported base image, or disk inputs can be destructive or require an explicit rebuild. Always inspect the plan.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: nodes maps stable names to VM IDs, roles, and addresses. ansible_inventory contains one k3s_server, three k3s_agents, SSH username, guest Python path, cluster CIDRs, and the service subnet's host-10 DNS address. Neither output contains passwords, private keys, Kubernetes tokens, or kubeconfig data.

docs.title: Controller Environment
docs.text:
Variable Purpose PROXMOX_VE_ENDPOINT Verified HTTPS URL, including port 8006 PROXMOX_VE_API_TOKEN Dedicated API credential in provider format user@realm!token=secret ANSIBLE_CONFIG Normally unset; the root configuration is selected automatically ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD_FILE Optional absolute path outside Git; mode 0600 SSL_CERT_FILE Optional verified CA bundle for Python tooling behind a private CA UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=true Use system trust when installing controller tools behind a private CA

Never set provider insecure mode, disable SSH host checks, or turn off Kubernetes TLS validation to get past a trust failure. Install the correct CA or verify the host fingerprint instead.

docs.title: Vault Schema
docs.text:
make vault generates and encrypts these fields without writing plaintext:

Key Requirement k3s_token 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters; preserve the original for restore grafana_admin_password At least 24 characters; generated value is longer desktop_password_hash Optional SHA-512-crypt ($6$) or yescrypt ($y$) hash

The desktop password hash enables console login only. Without it, Desktop still boots, but the ubuntu password remains locked. Grafana's secret is a bootstrap credential: changing it does not reset an already-initialized Grafana database.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Effect Live resources? make setup Install frozen Python dependencies and pinned local collections No make init Initialize Terraform provider/backend No mutation of VMs make plan Refresh and preview VM changes Reads Proxmox make apply Apply after Terraform confirmation Yes make inventory Validate Terraform outputs and write private JSON inventory Reads state make vault Prompt for vault password and create encrypted credentials No make configure Reconcile Desktop, K3s, kubeconfig, and monitoring Yes make kube-shell Open a controller shell with this lab's kubeconfig selected No mutation of cluster resources make verify Check nodes, versions, workloads, PVCs, health, scrape targets, Helm test Read checks plus temporary Helm test pod make idempotence Apply once, then require zero changes on a full second run Yes make replace-worker NODE=pn51-worker-2 Plan, guard, confirm, drain, and replace only that worker Yes; destroys its root disk make destroy Destroy managed VMs, disks, and image after confirmation Yes; destructive make lint Terraform formatting, Ruff, and production Ansible lint No make chart-check Verify checksum, lint/render real chart, parse CRDs No make test-templates Render actual Ansible templates twice for four fake guests No make test Mocked Terraform, chart, template, and Python tests No make check Lint, tests, and strict documentation build No make secrets-scan Redacted Gitleaks scan of Git history No make docs / make docs-serve Build / preview documentation No

VAULT_FILE defaults to .local/vault.yml. VAULT_ARGS defaults to --ask-vault-pass; a password-file workflow can use make configure VAULT_ARGS='--vault-password-file /absolute/private/path'. CONFIG_FILE is unset by default; set it to .local/config.yml for optional non-secret Ansible settings. Both configuration and idempotence runs use the same file. Secret values still belong in the encrypted vault, not Make arguments. UV can select a different uv executable. Do not put secret values in Make arguments or extra-vars strings.

docs.title: Optional Dotfiles
docs.text:
The sibling dotfiles repository owns user configuration and its node package manifest. Homelab fetches a pinned public commit and delegates configuration to that repository; it does not copy workstation dotfiles or private overrides.

Variable Default Contract dotfiles_enabled false Enable explicitly through your private configuration dotfiles_repository Public TheNewThinkTank dotfiles HTTPS Git URL Credential-free GitHub URL dotfiles_revision b703d09fe26c5bd7e9daac92450f3c313a4c7c6a Reviewed full lowercase 40-character published commit SHA dotfiles_profile personal personal or work; independent of package selection dotfiles_home /home/ubuntu Guest account boundary; the role rejects another home dotfiles_checkout /home/ubuntu/.local/share/dotfiles/source User-owned source, never root's personal configuration

The role requires the new --check and --package-set interfaces from the selected commit and always selects the lightweight homelab package set. It does not invoke a full workstation package installer on every run. Ansible owns APT convergence; dotfiles owns the package names, plugins, configuration, backup/restore, and official kubectl version/checksums.

kubectl is downloaded directly from dl.k8s.io, verified by SHA-256, and checked against its declared version. The selected client must be within one Kubernetes minor of K3s. An existing unrelated user-local binary is preserved and causes a clear failure rather than a silent replacement. Updating the pin may require an explicit, backed-up binary migration.

Configuration and plugin checks return 0 when current, 3 when changes are needed, and another nonzero status on errors. Ansible installs only missing plugins and deploys configuration only after a real content difference. An unchanged second run creates no new configuration backups. Full live acceptance remains required.

docs.title: Public Repository Security
docs.text: The public repository contains desired configuration, public examples, non-secret version/checksum pins, and tests. Your controller and Proxmox host remain the trust boundary; GitHub Actions never deploys infrastructure.

docs.title: Credentials and State
docs.text:
Material Storage Rule Proxmox API token Controller environment or password manager Dedicated, scoped token; never tfvars SSH private key SSH agent or private key store outside Git Never generated by Terraform SSH public key Ignored local tfvars; passed to cloud-init Public, but keep personal key metadata out of examples K3s token and Grafana bootstrap password Encrypted .local/vault.yml Vault password stored separately Optional desktop password hash Same encrypted vault Hashes are sensitive offline-cracking targets Kubeconfig .local/kubeconfig, mode 0600 Cluster-administrator credential Terraform state and saved plans Ignored local files or a private locked backend Treat all state and plans as sensitive Idempotence reports .local/idempotence.json, mode 0600 May include operational metadata; never CI artifacts etcd snapshots and VM backups Encrypted off-host storage Contain credentials and application data

sensitive = true is output redaction, not encryption. This repository avoids Terraform password/private-key resources and Kubernetes/Helm providers so those credentials never enter its state. Provider credentials come from environment variables. State still reveals network topology and infrastructure metadata and must be protected.

For one operator, an encrypted workstation disk and encrypted off-host state backup are the default. For collaboration, use a private remote backend with encryption, versioning, and locking. Configure backend authentication outside Git and migrate existing state deliberately with terraform init -migrate-state. Never run concurrent operators against independent copies of local state.

Ansible secret tasks use no_log, suppress diffs, avoid cached token facts, and keep token/config files root-only. No plaintext vault file is created by the generation helper. Decrypting or editing a vault is a separate trusted operator action; your editor and workstation must also be protected.

docs.title: Network Policy at the VM Boundary
docs.text:
The Proxmox datacenter firewall must be active. All four VM NICs enable firewall processing and each VM defaults to dropping inbound traffic:

Source Destination Allowed Explicit admin_cidrs All guests TCP 22 Explicit admin_cidrs Server only TCP 6443 Four exact node addresses All nodes UDP 8472 for Flannel, TCP 10250 for kubelet, ICMP Four exact node addresses Server only TCP 6443 Guest outbound Package/image registries, DNS, time, other destinations Allowed; replies are statefully tracked

Flannel VXLAN is not encrypted. Keep this LAN/VLAN trusted and do not expose UDP 8472 to the internet. VM firewalls do not isolate pods from one another: application namespaces still need appropriate Kubernetes NetworkPolicies and RBAC. This baseline intentionally does not claim a zero-trust pod network.

No NodePort range, load-balancer controller, ingress controller, host metrics port, RDP, or VNC network service is opened. Grafana and Prometheus are ClusterIP-only; use loopback port forwarding. Public ingress and an authentication proxy need a separate explicit design.

Guest UFW is not configured by this workflow. Do not apply an old generic UFW or hardening script over the cluster: forwarding rules and strict reverse-path filtering can break the CNI. The network boundary is outside the guests.

docs.title: Host and Cluster Privileges
docs.text:
The cloud-init ubuntu account has passwordless sudo, because Ansible must configure the guests without embedding sudo credentials. Treat its SSH key as a guest-root credential. Root SSH and password SSH are disabled. An optional console password does not re-enable password SSH.

K3s enables Secret encryption at rest and protects kubeconfig/token permissions. Workers join with the running server's CA-pinned secure token, not only a short bootstrap password. Existing token mismatch and stale worker identity checks fail closed. Token rotation and etcd restores are deliberate operations, not automatic convergence.

The monitoring namespace permits privileged pod security because node-exporter needs host inspection. Do not allow untrusted workloads or namespace-admin users there. Keep application namespaces restricted separately. Grafana Secret values are outside Helm release values, but remain Kubernetes Secrets: base64 is not encryption and cluster administrators can read them.

docs.title: How to Check Before Publishing
docs.text:
git status --short
git check-ignore pn51/terraform/terraform.tfvars .local/vault.yml .local/kubeconfig
make secrets-scan

Review staged files and diffs before committing. The working-tree secret scan uses Git's tracked and nonignored file list, so it includes new public source without scanning private runtime data. A direct gitleaks dir can also flag legitimate credentials in ignored private directories on an operator's machine. Never upload raw output or solve that by committing those directories or globally disabling rules. No path-based scanner exception is added to hide tracked secrets.

Git ignore rules do not protect a file that was already committed. Remove the file from tracking, rotate the exposed credential immediately, then coordinate history cleanup as needed. Deleting the latest file does not remove it from Git history or forks. The existing application Secret example has empty values; populate real application secrets through a separate secret-management workflow.

docs.title: How to Rotate Secrets
docs.text:
Rotate the Proxmox token in Proxmox, update the controller secret store, test a plan, then revoke the old token. Rotate SSH keys by adding and testing a new public key before removing the old one; cloud-init is first-boot configuration, so existing guests may need an explicit authorized-keys update or rebuild.

K3s server-token rotation changes datastore bootstrap protection: follow the K3s token procedure, update the encrypted vault and root token files deliberately, and take a new snapshot. Preserve old tokens with snapshots that require them. The role deliberately refuses an unexplained token change on an existing node.

Grafana reads its initial admin password into its persistent database. Rotating only the Kubernetes Secret does not change that database password. Use Grafana's documented account-administration flow, update the vault, and verify login. Never put a new password in a CLI argument that will be logged.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Trust failures require correct CAs or verified host fingerprints, not insecure flags. Unexpected secret-scan findings require a local review with redacted output. Restore failures involving tokens require the snapshot's original token, not an attempt to brute-force a fresh credential into the datastore.

See provisioning, operations, and testing.

docs.title: Testing and Acceptance
docs.text: There are two different claims to verify: the source describes a coherent lab, and that lab actually converges on your PN51. CI proves the first. Only live acceptance and recovery exercises can prove the second.

docs.title: Credential-Free Gates
docs.text:
make setup
make check

The chart download and dependency installation require internet access, but no Proxmox, SSH, vault, or Kubernetes credentials. Tests never call Terraform apply against the host.

Gate Evidence Terraform fmt/validate Configuration matches the pinned real provider schema Terraform mocked plans Exactly four VMs; one server/three workers; default RAM budget; firewalls; deterministic inventory Negative Terraform cases World-open administration, small Desktop RAM, gateway/IP collisions, overlapping networks, private-key input rejected Ansible production lint Fully qualified modules, schema/syntax, task conventions, YAML formatting Real Ansible templates All four host configs rendered; server/agent flag separation; token-file use; unchanged second render Python regressions Private modes, symlinks, vault encryption/failure, inventory precedence, replacement scope and PV guards, idempotence evidence Dotfiles role contracts Mutable revisions rejected before package installation; public source and ubuntu ownership; local configuration fixture changes only when necessary Real pinned chart Exact archive checksum; strict Helm lint; render against pinned Kubernetes version; private services; persistent storage; existing Grafana Secret CRD regression All ten real CRDs parse safely; YAML = scalar handled without Python-object construction MkDocs strict Navigation and local documentation links build without warnings Secret scanning Redacted Git-history scan in CI; tracked and nonignored working files scanned before publication

The GitHub workflow pins its actions to commit IDs, uses a frozen Python lockfile, and grants infrastructure validation read-only repository access. It has no homelab credentials or self-hosted runner. Documentation publishing has its own separate write-capable workflow.

docs.title: How to Run Live Acceptance
docs.text:
After initial configuration:

make verify

This requires the private inventory/kubeconfig and a reachable cluster. It checks all declared node names, exact K3s versions and Ready conditions, monitoring Deployment/StatefulSet/DaemonSet replica health, three Bound persistent claims, Grafana's database health, nonempty healthy Prometheus targets, and helm test. Helm test creates a temporary chart test pod; it does not rebuild VMs.

Also inspect the Desktop console on all guests, confirm the Proxmox datacenter firewall is enforcing the declared policy, and verify that a non-admin machine cannot reach guest SSH or the server API. An internal cluster health check cannot prove an external firewall is enabled.

docs.title: How to Prove Full Convergence
docs.text:
make idempotence

The first run establishes desired state. The second full run writes a private JSON callback report and must show zero changes, failures, unreachable hosts, rescued tasks, and ignored failures on the exact four expected hosts. An empty report, missing host, or partial --limit run cannot pass the evidence checker.

The report stays under ignored .local/; do not upload it as a public artifact. When dotfiles is enabled, run make idempotence CONFIG_FILE=.local/config.yml. The role checks package state, missing plugins, and managed configuration separately; it does not hide a full bootstrap behind an always-unchanged command. If a task changes again, inspect that exact task rather than hiding it with a blanket changed_when: false. Pure observation commands are intentionally unchanged; actual package, Secret, file, service, and Helm changes are not hidden.

docs.title: How to Exercise Recovery
docs.text: On an isolated test copy, prove that a stateless worker can be replaced and rejoin under its original name, that a data-bearing worker is refused, and that etcd plus application data can be restored from off-host backups. Run live acceptance and idempotence after each exercise. Never test a production restore against conflicting VM IDs or addresses.

docs.title: Verification Limits
docs.text:
Mocked plans do not prove Proxmox ACLs, imported-image boot behavior, guest-agent startup, Ubuntu Desktop installation, CNI traffic, kernel compatibility, or physical capacity. Chart rendering does not prove successful operator scheduling or database migration. Local template convergence is not a substitute for the full live second-run check.

The repository deliberately does not claim those live results until you run the gates on your host. Known controller collection deprecation warnings are not suppressed globally; review them when updating pinned dependencies.

The sibling dotfiles project has independent offline and real-plugin tests for MacBook personal/work profiles. Its Ubuntu 26.04 CI covers both the workstation and lightweight homelab package sets. With Docker running, use DOTFILES_PACKAGE_SET=homelab make ubuntu there to test the lightweight native installer. A passing local Ansible fixture does not prove the full VM deployment or replace those native Linux checks.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Run the failing slice directly with make lint, make chart-check, make test-templates, or uv run --frozen python -m pytest. Use terraform -chdir=pn51/terraform test for mocked plans. For a live failure, inspect node/pod events and the exact failing Ansible task without enabling secret-bearing debug output.

See operations, reference, and monitoring troubleshooting.

docs.title: Asus PN51
docs.text: Component Target CPU AMD Ryzen 7 5700U, 8 cores / 16 threads Graphics Integrated Radeon Vega; guests use virtual displays, not GPU passthrough Network Gigabit Ethernet, existing private LAN or VLAN Memory 32 GiB Storage 1 TB Samsung 980 NVMe Hypervisor Proxmox VE 9 on bare metal

docs.title: Resource Budget
docs.text:
Guest Role vCPU RAM Disk pn51-server-1 K3s control plane and embedded etcd 2 6 GiB 80 GiB pn51-worker-1 K3s worker 2 6 GiB 80 GiB pn51-worker-2 K3s worker 2 6 GiB 80 GiB pn51-worker-3 K3s worker 2 6 GiB 80 GiB

Ubuntu Desktop runs on every guest, including the control plane. The full ubuntu-desktop package installs GNOME and GDM; this is not a server-only installation with a misleading name. A cloud image is the reproducible starting point rather than an interactive ISO installer.

The administrator can use Proxmox's virtual console. Console login remains password-locked unless a password hash is supplied through the vault. SSH uses your existing keys and remains password-disabled even when console login is enabled.

The control plane is tainted to keep ordinary workloads on workers. Desktop and monitoring consume real resources: this baseline is appropriate for learning and small services, not four simultaneous heavy desktop sessions or large LLMs.

See architecture, provisioning, and configuration reference.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Git[Public Git repository] --> CI[Credential-free validation]
    Git --> Controller[Trusted administrator workstation]
    Controller -->|Terraform: verified HTTPS API| Proxmox[Proxmox VE 9 on PN51]
    Proxmox -->|Cloud-init: key and static address| Guests[Four Ubuntu 26.04 guests]
    Controller -->|Ansible: verified SSH| Guests
    Guests --> Desktop[Ubuntu Desktop and guest baseline]
    Guests --> Cluster[K3s: one server and three workers]
    Controller -->|Helm through verified Kubernetes API| Monitoring[Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager]
    Cluster --> Monitoring

GitHub Actions validates source and scans Git history. It cannot reach the homelab and receives no Proxmox token, SSH key, vault password, or kubeconfig. The separate documentation publisher only writes the documentation branch.

Terraform owns VM identity, CPU, RAM, disks, virtual displays, static addressing, the imported image, and VM firewall rules. Cloud-init owns the initial ubuntu account and authorized public keys. Ansible waits for cloud-init to finish, then owns the desktop, guest baseline, K3s service, and monitoring release.

The private Ansible inventory comes from Terraform output. CIDRs and the cluster DNS address travel through that inventory rather than being duplicated in group variables. Helm release credentials are not stored in Terraform state.

docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Admin[Trusted administration subnet] -->|22 and server 6443 only| Bridge[Existing private bridge or VLAN]
    subgraph PN51[PN51: one physical failure domain]
        Host[Proxmox: 8 GiB RAM reserved]
        Bridge --> Server[server-1: Desktop, K3s, single-member etcd]
        Bridge --> Worker1[worker-1: Desktop and K3s agent]
        Bridge --> Worker2[worker-2: Desktop and K3s agent]
        Bridge --> Worker3[worker-3: Desktop and K3s agent]
        Server <-->|6443, 10250, UDP 8472| Worker1
        Server <-->|6443, 10250, UDP 8472| Worker2
        Server <-->|6443, 10250, UDP 8472| Worker3
        Worker1 --- LocalStorage[Node-local persistent volumes]
        Worker2 --- LocalStorage
        Worker3 --- LocalStorage
    end
    LocalStorage --> OffHost[Operator-managed off-host backups]
    Server --> OffHost

All node pairs also exchange VXLAN and kubelet traffic where required. The diagram abbreviates those links. No etcd ports or NodePort range are exposed between VMs: this is not a multi-server etcd cluster, and applications are not published by default.

docs.title: Why These Choices
docs.text:
Decision Reason Cost Proxmox rather than nested local virtualization Dedicated VM lifecycle, bridge networking, console, backups, API imports One manual, potentially destructive host installation Full Desktop on all VMs Meets the desktop requirement with inspectable virtual consoles Larger memory, disk, update, and attack-surface budget than Server Cloud image plus Ansible Checksummed base and repeatable package state without interactive installers First desktop installation needs network access and time K3s rather than kubeadm Bundled runtime, CNI, storage bootstrap, and lower operational overhead K3s-specific configuration and upgrade procedures One server and three workers Leaves three workload nodes and a simple recovery model API outage on server restart; no control-plane HA Embedded etcd Native scheduled snapshots and a documented restore path One member is not redundant storage Proxmox VM firewall Filters outside guest container networking Requires the datacenter firewall enabled and verified Local-path storage Small footprint and no pretend redundancy on one NVMe disk A data-bearing VM cannot be replaced without data work Vault and existing SSH keys No credential generation or Kubernetes authentication in Terraform Vault password and backups remain operator responsibilities

Three control-plane VMs on this same host would tolerate a guest failure, but not a PN51 power, network, or disk failure. For useful HA, add independent physical hosts and storage before increasing control-plane count.

docs.title: Reconciliation and Recovery
docs.text:
Normal configuration runs do not perform unconditional package upgrades, reboot nodes, rotate credentials, or restart SSH/K3s. Templates and checksums notify handlers only when their inputs change. Workers are updated serially and drained before K3s changes; disruption budgets are respected.

Worker replacement is intentionally separate from reconciliation. Its helper checks node-local volumes, checks the remaining nodes, validates the complete Terraform plan, and asks for an exact typed confirmation. Control-plane replacement requires snapshot recovery.

The design is declarative at its ownership boundaries, not a promise that state can be thrown away. Preserve the Terraform state, vault, original server token, etcd snapshots, and application backups outside the PN51.

See the input reference and security boundaries.

docs.title: Guest Baseline
docs.text: The Ansible baseline role is the only supported guest-bootstrap path. Do not run the former one-off hardening scripts over these nodes; their UFW, reverse-path filtering, package-upgrade, and service behavior conflict with this design.

docs.title: Enforced State
docs.text:
• Ubuntu 26.04 x86-64 guest and minimum-memory assertions, after cloud-init.
  • Full Desktop, OpenSSH, AppArmor, guest agent, and security-update packages.
  • Public-key SSH only, no root SSH, low authentication-attempt limit, early drop-in precedence, and configuration validation before a conditional reload.
  • Root-only K3s config/token and administrator kubeconfig; no token in systemd arguments or Terraform state.
  • Persisted bridge-netfilter/overlay modules, forwarding enabled, and CNI-safe reverse-path filtering. Kubernetes kernel-protection defaults are explicit.
  • Swap removed from active state and fstab; desktop sleep/suspend targets masked.
  • Security updates enabled without automatic reboots.
  • Desktop graphical target enabled; optional vaulted console password hash does not enable password SSH.

VM ingress is enforced by Proxmox, not by duplicating iptables policy with guest UFW. Keep the datacenter firewall active and validate the boundary from another machine. AppArmor remains enabled; this is not a CIS certification claim.

docs.title: How to Verify the Baseline
docs.text:
Run make configure, inspect the guests' Desktop consoles, then run make verify and make idempotence. On each guest, inspect SSH's effective configuration with sudo sshd -T, swap with swapon --show, and the boot target with systemctl get-default.

If networking fails, inspect the exact Proxmox rules, kernel settings, CNI pods, and routes before adding broad allow rules. If SSH hardening fails validation, keep the existing verified connection open and repair the failing setting.

See security boundaries, testing, and maintenance.

docs.title: Threat Model
docs.text: This lab assumes a trusted administrator workstation, a private trusted node network, a patched Proxmox host, and Ubuntu/GitHub/Helm artifacts obtained through verified TLS and pinned checksums where supported.

docs.title: What the Baseline Addresses
docs.text: Risk Control Public Git credential exposure Ignored local artifacts, Vault, no private-key generation in Terraform, history scans Accidental network exposure Default-drop VM ingress, explicit administrator CIDRs, no public monitoring services Man-in-the-middle administration Proxmox CA trust, verified SSH host keys, Kubernetes CA validation, secure worker join token Configuration drift Declarative roles, handlers, mock/template tests, full live second-run acceptance Unintended destructive replacement Exact worker selection, PV guard, full-plan scope validation, typed confirmation Accidental cluster identity loss Stable inventory, stale-node detection, token mismatch guard, documented restore requirements

docs.title: What Remains an Operator Responsibility
docs.text:
One machine cannot provide physical high availability. Its NVMe disk and local volumes are not replicated. Scheduled local etcd snapshots are not off-host backups. A compromised administrator key, Proxmox host, or cluster-admin kubeconfig can control the lab.

Desktop increases the guest package and GUI attack surface. Node-exporter needs host inspection; its namespace permits privileged pod security. VXLAN traffic is private-network traffic, not an encrypted overlay. The cluster does not claim default-deny pod-to-pod policy or application-level authentication.

Do not publish workloads until you have designed namespace RBAC, appropriate NetworkPolicies, ingress TLS/authentication, dependency updates, and application backup/restore. PodSecurityPolicy is removed from modern Kubernetes; use Pod Security Admission and current policy tooling instead.

See the enforced guest baseline, secret and network controls, and backup/restore procedures.
